When building agents, the context window matters because it limits how much conversation history, code, documentation, or tool results you can keep in active memory; once you exceed it, older information gets dropped or compressed away. runs.result_text: An LLM's **context window** is the maximum amount of text (measured in tokens, roughly 4 characters per token) the model can process in a single request—everything you give it plus everything it generates. For Claude, this ranges from 100K tokens (Haiku) to 200K (Opus). When building agents, context windows matter because they determine how much **history, instructions, and tool results** you can keep in memory simultaneously. A small window forces you to summarize or discard past work (expensive context switches, lost state); a large window lets agents maintain rich awareness of prior decisions, failures, and patterns without losing focus. For multi-step agent tasks, running out of context mid-task means you either lose context and restart, or you're forced to use external persistence (files, databases) to hand off state—which adds latency and coordination complexity. Good agent architecture respects your actual context limit by being deliberate about what stays hot (recent decisions, active context) versus what gets persisted (archives, memory systems).

runs.result_text:
An LLM's context window is the maximum number of tokens (roughly words) it can process in a single request—essentially the amount of text it can "see" at once. For Claude 5.5 models, this ranges from 128K to 200K tokens depending on the model tier.

When building agents, context window matters because:
- **Agent memory & history**: Agents with longer conversations eat more tokens; a small window forces frequent "handoffs" or memory pruning
- **Tool definitions & state**: Every available tool, skill, system prompt, and user request consumes tokens—larger windows let you wire in more tools or pass richer context
- **Cost & latency**: Larger context = slower processing and higher token costs, so you trade capability for speed/expense
- **Cache efficiency**: Claude's prompt caching charges 90% less for cached tokens (after first request), making it possible to keep substantial context cheap if it's reused

For agent work, this means: keep the core system prompt tight, load only relevant context via memory/skills when triggered, use caching for stable context (like skill definitions), and design handoffs to reset context on major shifts—that's how MARVIN stays responsive despite managing dozens of skills and cross-session memory.
